title: Rabies Exposure and Vietnam’s Uninspected Dog Supply Chain
excerpt: A rabid dog attacked four people in Đắk Lắk on September 7. Untracked transport and slaughter leave families, workers, and animals outside basic biosecurity.
body_html:
On September 7, 2026, health authorities in Đắk Lắk confirmed that a dog which attacked four people in Bình Kiến ward tested positive for rabies. The incident involved household exposure, not a proven dog-meat shipment. But it shows why rabies protection cannot stop at property gates.

Rabies spreads mainly through infected saliva entering the body through bites or scratches. Once clinical symptoms appear, it is virtually 100% fatal. After exposure, people need immediate wound washing with soap and water, followed urgently by rabies vaccine and serum before symptoms develop. Delay can kill.

Broken barriers multiply risk

Hanoi CDC has warned residents not to slaughter, eat, or use meat or products from animals suspected of rabies, and to report suspicious dogs or cats to authorities. Properly cooked meat is not an established rabies transmission route. Risk rises through bites, handling sick animals, uninspected slaughter, and contact with contaminated saliva or tissues.

Illicit dog pipelines create another biosecurity gap. Animals moved across provincial borders without reliable identification, quarantine, or veterinary inspection can reach handlers, slaughter sites, and households without traceable health records. This does not prove every traded animal carries rabies. It proves an unregulated chain weakens prevention.

Enforcement must lead to abolition

Vietnam recorded 164 animal rabies outbreaks across 129 communes and wards in 22 provinces and cities by September 3, with 51 human deaths reported nationwide. These figures demand vaccination, registration, rapid exposure treatment, and criminal action against theft and illegal transport. Such tools must dismantle the supply chain, not preserve it through permanent regulation.

Vietnam has no national law banning the dog-meat trade. Communities already protect companion animals as family, and a 2023 Four Paws/local survey reported roughly 95% rejection of the trade. SDE calls for complete national abolition by 2030. Sign the national petition and support Vietnamese families, veterinary workers, and local authorities demanding a safer, cruelty-free future.
